paragraphs: When some classes appear much more often than others, a learning system can perform poorly on the rare classes. Incorrect annotations compound this problem. This paper studies active learning under both conditions: deciding which examples should receive annotation so that a limited labeling budget supports informative learning and better class balance.

The proposed framework uses prior knowledge from a foundation model together with decisions from a smaller model. Their joint selection process accounts for class imbalance while identifying useful examples to annotate. The central idea is that sample selection should consider both what the models can learn from an example and how the selected data represent underrepresented classes.

Experiments cover imbalanced image and text datasets with noisy labels. The authors report annotation savings of more than 50% relative to the best active learning baseline while preserving performance and robustness to label noise. These findings support combining foundation-model knowledge with targeted sample selection when annotation resources are limited and the existing labels are unevenly distributed or unreliable.
icml-2026-active-learning-with-foundatio.tldr: A foundation model and a smaller model jointly select informative, class-aware examples, saving over 50% of annotations in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: An agent’s initial plan can become less useful as a long task develops. AdaMEM addresses this problem by making experience-based guidance adaptive during execution. The paper targets memory systems that retrieve past experience only at the beginning of an episode, leaving the agent with guidance that may no longer fit its current situation.

AdaMEM combines two kinds of memory. A long-term store contains raw trajectories collected offline, while a short-term store generates strategies as the task unfolds. This changes the agent’s behavior without updating its model parameters online. The architecture also supports a trade-off between the tokens spent on adaptation and the flexibility of the resulting guidance.

The authors report relative gains of up to 13% on ALFWorld and 11% on WebShop over static memory baselines, alongside leading results on HotpotQA agentic search. They additionally introduce Step-MFT, which trains the policy to turn retrieved experiences into better strategies. Its further gains suggest that adaptive retrieval and the ability to interpret retrieved experience can both contribute to stronger agents.
icml-2026-adamem-test-time-adaptive-memo.tldr: AdaMEM updates experience-based strategies during task execution, improving agent adaptation without online parameter updates.

paragraphs: Statistical learning theory studies how learning from finite data can support reliable predictions. This paper builds a formal foundation for that theory in Lean 4, where mathematical arguments are expressed as proofs that can be checked by the system. Its focus is empirical process theory, which supplies tools for analyzing fluctuations between observed data and underlying distributions.

The project develops several missing pieces of the Lean library: Gaussian Lipschitz concentration, Dudley’s entropy integral theorem for sub-Gaussian processes, and an application to least-squares regression, including sparse regression, with a sharp rate. These results form a connected infrastructure that links probabilistic tools to a concrete learning-theory application.

Humans designed the proof strategies, while AI agents constructed tactical proof steps within a human-verified workflow. Formalization also exposed implicit assumptions and omitted details in standard textbook arguments, which the project resolved. The contribution is therefore both a reusable mathematical toolbox and a more explicit account of why its results hold, providing groundwork for further formal developments in machine learning theory.
icml-2026-ai4slt-empirical-processes-in-.tldr: AI4SLT formalizes core empirical-process results and regression theory in Lean 4 through a human–AI proof-building workflow.

paragraphs: CauchyNet targets regression functions with sharp, rational-like spikes and inputs that are only partially observed. Such patterns can require wide standard real-valued networks. The proposed alternative is a compact complex-valued network whose hidden units multiply shifted reciprocal features, giving its architecture a direct connection to Cauchy-type kernel representations.

The theoretical result establishes that finite sums of multivariate Cauchy kernels can approximate continuous functions arbitrarily closely on compact subsets of real-valued input space. The authors also show how CauchyNet can represent those sums through its complex biases and output weights. This connects the network’s construction to a broad approximation property, rather than relying solely on empirical performance.

In the reported experiments, CauchyNet achieves lower errors on near-singular functions and gap-filling tasks, often using substantially fewer trainable parameters. Results on smooth and piecewise-affine functions are mixed. That distinction helps identify the intended use case: the architecture is especially motivated by sharply varying rational-like behavior, while the experiments do not establish a uniform advantage across function types.
icml-2026-cauchynet-compact-and-data-eff.tldr: CauchyNet uses complex reciprocal features to model sharp regression functions compactly, with mixed results on smoother target functions.

paragraphs: Long reasoning traces can contain complex dependencies, making their quality difficult to assess as a simple sequence of text. This paper connects three problems: defining good reasoning, evaluating its internal structure, and using that evaluation to improve model behavior. Its ME² principle considers both efficiency and effectiveness at the level of individual reasoning steps and the overall trace.

The authors represent reasoning traces as directed acyclic graphs, allowing evaluation to account for dependencies within an argument. They build a pairwise evaluation method around this representation, then use it to create the TRM-Preference dataset. A Thinking Reward Model trained on that dataset provides a scalable signal for assessing reasoning quality.

The experiments apply thinking rewards in two settings. Selecting better reasoning at inference time produces reported gains of up to 19.3%, while using the rewards during reinforcement learning produces gains of up to 3.9% across diverse tasks. The findings support evaluating the reasoning process itself as a useful signal for both choosing among candidate solutions and improving subsequent training.
icml-2026-characterizing-evaluating-and-.tldr: A graph-based account of reasoning quality trains a reward model that improves both inference-time selection and reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning for reasoning faces a moving data-selection problem: examples that offer a useful challenge today can become trivial as the model improves. The paper focuses on the scarcity of medium-difficulty training examples and the need to keep that difficulty aligned with the learner’s changing capabilities.

D²Evo pairs a Solver with a Questioner and updates both across training iterations. It first identifies medium-difficulty anchor examples using the current Solver’s abilities. The Questioner then learns to generate diverse questions at suitable difficulty levels from those anchors. Joint optimization allows question generation to evolve alongside solving ability, addressing the mismatch that can arise when generated training data do not track the learner.

The authors report better performance than existing methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks while using fewer than 2,000 real mathematical samples. They also report strong generalization on general reasoning benchmarks. These results support an adaptive data-generation loop in which the value of a question depends on the current learner, rather than treating difficulty as a fixed property throughout training.
icml-2026-d-2-evo-dual-difficulty-aware-.tldr: D²Evo jointly trains a question generator and solver so generated reasoning problems stay appropriately challenging as the solver improves.

paragraphs: Fair classification becomes more complicated when predictions have several possible classes. Methods developed for binary decisions do not straightforwardly capture the richer output structure and fairness constraints. This paper asks what accuracy is optimally achievable under those constraints and how practical algorithms can approach that accuracy–fairness boundary.

The authors first give an analytically tractable probabilistic description of the optimal fair classifier. They then derive two attribute-blind algorithms for different intervention points. An in-processing method incorporates fairness during training through a reduction approach. A post-processing method instead adjusts output probabilities using plug-in estimation, providing a route for intervening after the underlying classifier has been trained.

The theoretical analysis establishes convergence of both methods to the optimal accuracy–fairness Pareto frontier in the paper’s formulation. This frontier describes trade-offs where improving one objective requires sacrificing the other. Experiments on multiple datasets show a stronger balance between accuracy and fairness than the compared methods. Together, the results connect a characterization of the optimum with algorithms designed to attain it.
icml-2026-demystifying-the-optimal-fair-.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal multiclass accuracy–fairness trade-offs and develops training-time and post-processing algorithms that converge to that frontier.

paragraphs: A time series can contain both slowly varying behavior and brief, localized events. DualTimesField builds this distinction into its representation, describing the signal over continuous time as a combination of smooth trends and discrete events. The approach addresses difficulties with irregular sampling, representation cost, and the tendency of traditional implicit neural representations to mix different frequencies.

The framework uses two implicit neural fields with different responsibilities. A Continuous Time Field captures smooth trends through a bandwidth-limited parameterization. A Discrete Geometric Field represents transient events with learnable Gabor atoms, gated sparsity, and a scale schedule that progresses from coarse to fine. This separation gives sustained behavior and short-lived changes distinct modeling mechanisms.

Across nine real-world benchmarks, the authors report a 51.2% average reduction in mean squared error relative to discrete-time baselines, together with competitive interpolation on irregularly sampled data. The findings support explicitly separating trends from events as a way to improve reconstruction fidelity while retaining a continuous-time representation suited to observations that do not arrive at uniform intervals.
icml-2026-dualtimesfield-rethinking-time.tldr: DualTimesField represents time series with separate continuous-time fields for smooth trends and transient events, improving reported reconstruction accuracy.

paragraphs: Text diffusion generation needs to balance producing faithful outputs with exploring meaningfully different possibilities. Adjusting individual token probabilities does not necessarily capture whether the resulting text is semantically repetitive. This paper introduces Semantic-Aware Kernel Entropy, or SAKE, a training-free guidance method that incorporates relationships among tokens and their relative positions.

SAKE measures order-2 Rényi entropy using a kernel Gram matrix that reflects those semantic and positional relationships. The authors linearize this objective in embedding space to obtain a manageable guidance signal for sampling. When generation becomes redundant, the signal flattens the sampling distribution to encourage exploration; when diversity is already present, it sharpens the distribution to support fidelity.

The experiments show a better empirical fidelity–diversity Pareto frontier than temperature scaling and discrete guidance baselines. They also report improved performance when generating multiple candidate answers for reasoning-heavy tasks, including code and mathematics. The result suggests that guidance informed by semantic relationships can make multiple samples more useful, rather than merely making their token choices more random.
icml-2026-exploring-more-to-solve-more-b.tldr: SAKE guides text diffusion with semantic entropy, improving the measured balance between output fidelity, diversity, and multi-sample reasoning performance.

paragraphs: Compressing a time-series foundation model by copying its individual features can tie the smaller model closely to the teacher’s particular training history. This paper instead distills a shared geometric structure, motivated by observations that high-level representations across model sizes tend toward an approximately low-rank geometry and that layer usefulness is unevenly distributed.

The method selects influential teacher layers, estimates a stabilized covariance of their embeddings, and extracts a low-dimensional consensus subspace. During student training, it matches the mean and covariance of representations projected into that subspace. This provides statistical alignment without requiring point-by-point feature imitation. A further frequency-domain mechanism injects uncertainty within the consensus directions to mitigate bias introduced by selecting only a subset of layers.

The student matches or slightly improves on its teacher in forecasting and imputation, while showing a trade-off in strict zero-shot classification. With MOMENT-Large as teacher, the authors report about 90% fewer parameters and substantial distillation-time savings. The findings support transferring shared representation geometry as a practical compression target, with results differing across task types.
icml-2026-from-teacher-pathways-to-invar.tldr: Consensus subspace distillation compresses time-series models by matching shared representation statistics, achieving about 90% parameter reduction with MOMENT-Large.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can make mistakes when choosing tools or supplying arguments. Letting them discover those mistakes through real execution can be costly and can produce unwanted side effects. Gecko provides a simulation environment in which agents can revise their proposed tool calls before using the actual tools.

The simulator combines rules and language models to supply three kinds of feedback. It checks whether tool names and arguments are valid, generates responses that obey the tool schema and the current simulated state, and evaluates whether the sequence accomplishes the user’s objective. Maintaining state matters because a sequence of calls must remain coherent as earlier actions change the situation faced by later ones.

Using this feedback for iterative refinement yields GATS, a test-time scaling method that spends additional computation on simulated practice. On BFCLv3 and τ²-bench, GATS consistently improves multiple language models, including GPT-4o, GPT-5, and Gemini-3.0-pro. These results support stateful simulation as a useful source of corrective feedback for agent tool use before real execution.
icml-2026-gecko-a-simulation-environment.tldr: Gecko lets agents refine tool-call sequences using stateful simulated feedback, improving benchmark performance before real execution.

paragraphs: In-context learning adapts a model by placing demonstrations in its prompt, but a strict token budget limits how much guidance can fit. More examples are not automatically more useful when they repeat information or conflict. This paper treats prompt construction as selecting and compressing a finite-capacity message while preserving its task-relevant content.

The proposed RDCO optimizer is deterministic and requires no training. It scores each demonstration by the additional task information it contributes per token, while penalizing redundancy and conflicts conditioned on the existing prefix. After selection, it compacts the context subject to a bound on predictive divergence, controlling how much compression changes the predictive signal.

Across ten classification and structured-generation datasets, RDCO achieves average classification accuracy of 63.26 and generation exact match of 60.26. The reported improvements over the strongest respective baselines are 2.20 and 2.26 points, with a 4.94-point improvement in the ten-task overall average under the same budget. The findings support optimizing information density and compression jointly when prompt space is scarce.
icml-2026-in-context-learning-as-ratedis.tldr: RDCO selects and compresses demonstrations by task information per token, improving in-context learning under a fixed prompt budget.

paragraphs: Many multiclass unsupervised anomaly detectors train an encoder–decoder to reconstruct features of normal data and identify deviations from that reconstruction. This paper questions whether that task-specific training is necessary. It also highlights difficulties in reconstruction-based scoring and in training-free systems that mistakenly match features across unrelated categories or image regions.

Retrieval-based Anomaly Detection, or RAD, stores anomaly-free features in a memory and compares test patches against that memory through multi-level retrieval. The approach uses reference examples of normal appearance without training a model specifically for the anomaly-detection task. Its organizing principle is to detect unusual content through suitable feature matches to known normal data.

RAD achieves reported state-of-the-art performance on MVTec-AD, VisA, Real-IAD, and 3D-ADAM in both standard and few-shot settings. On MVTec-AD, its pixel AUROC is 96.7% with one anomaly-free image, compared with 98.5% using the full data. These results demonstrate that strong multiclass anomaly detection can be achieved through training-free memory retrieval in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-is-task-specific-training-nece.tldr: RAD detects anomalies by retrieving normal reference features, achieving leading reported results without task-specific training.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization offers a way to fine-tune language models without backpropagation, potentially reducing memory overhead. Its effectiveness depends on how it perturbs model parameters to guide updates. This paper targets a weakness of existing approaches: their sampling strategies are hand-designed and static, rather than adapted to a particular model’s structure.

ZO-Finetuner learns the perturbation strategy using a compact, memory-efficient optimizer. Its reuse strategy reflects the fact that the same base language model is often fine-tuned for many downstream tasks. The optimizer is trained once for that model and then reused across tasks with minimal overhead, spreading the cost of learning the optimization procedure across subsequent applications.

Experiments span four language models and seven datasets. ZO-Finetuner beats previous zeroth-order baselines in 82.1% of the evaluated task–model combinations. This supports learning model-specific optimization behavior as an effective alternative to fixed sampling rules. The reported comparison establishes broad success within those combinations while retaining the practical aim of fine-tuning without the memory demands of backpropagation.
icml-2026-learning-a-zeroth-order-optimi.tldr: ZO-Finetuner learns reusable, model-specific perturbation strategies for memory-efficient language-model fine-tuning without backpropagation.

paragraphs: Medical time-series classification requires recognizing local signal shapes, following longer-range dynamics, and accounting for relationships among measurement channels. Changes such as baseline drift can obscure useful patterns. MedMamba combines several architectural components to address these issues within an end-to-end state-space model.

First, convolutions at multiple scales encode local morphology. A three-branch encoder then processes the raw signal, temporal differences, and a frequency-domain view, combining them to emphasize informative patterns and suppress drift. A spatial graph Mamba module learns directed dependencies among channels. Its regularization encourages sparse connections and acyclicity, allowing the model to discover a dependency structure without requiring a predefined graph.

Across five real-world datasets, the authors report state-of-the-art classification performance while maintaining linear computational complexity. Ablation studies support the contribution of each component. The findings indicate that complementary signal views and learned channel relationships can work together: the temporal branches address changing signal behavior, while the graph component captures dependencies that treating channels independently would leave unmodeled.
icml-2026-medmamba-multi-view-state-spac.tldr: MedMamba combines multiple signal views with learned channel dependencies to improve medical time-series classification at linear computational complexity.

paragraphs: An external memory system can behave differently when information keeps arriving during use than when it is built once and queried afterward. Neuromem evaluates this streaming setting by interleaving new insertions with retrieval requests. The aim is to understand how the full memory lifecycle affects answer quality and the time required to serve queries.

The testbed separates five design choices: memory data structure, normalization, consolidation, query formulation, and integration of retrieved information into generation. It compares interchangeable variants within a shared serving stack on LoCoMo, LONGMEMEVAL, and MemAgentBench. Measurements include token-level F1 and insertion and retrieval latency, making both information quality and operational cost visible.

The authors observe that performance typically declines as memory grows across rounds, with time-related questions remaining the hardest category. The data structure largely determines the attainable quality frontier. Aggressive compression and generative integration mostly redistribute costs between inserting and retrieving information, with limited accuracy gains. These findings make evolving memory organization a central consideration when evaluating systems intended for continuous use.
icml-2026-neuromem-a-granular-decomposit.tldr: Neuromem benchmarks continuously growing language-model memory, revealing quality degradation and important trade-offs across the memory lifecycle.

paragraphs: Language models cache attention keys and values to avoid repeating computation, but this cache can dominate inference memory and bandwidth. Compressing it into very few bits risks accuracy loss because the values span a wide range. PatternKV addresses the overall distribution of cached vectors rather than focusing only on unusually large values.

The method identifies representative patterns online, associates each key or value vector with its nearest pattern, and quantizes the remaining difference. These residuals have a flatter distribution and a narrower range, improving the fidelity of low-bit representation. The approach draws on observed structure in keys that evolves with context and semantic regularities in values.

Across multiple models and long-context and test-time scaling settings, PatternKV reports consistent 2-bit gains and an average 4-bit drop of only 0.08% relative to FP16. It also reports a 10% average improvement in test-time scaling accuracy. Relative to FP16, throughput rises by 1.5 times and supported batch size by 1.25 times, connecting improved compression fidelity with practical inference capacity.
icml-2026-patternkv-flattening-kv-repres.tldr: PatternKV compresses attention caches by quantizing differences from shared patterns, improving low-bit accuracy and reported inference throughput.

paragraphs: Neural networks often favor solutions described as simple, but that description is difficult to turn into a broadly useful measurement. This paper measures simplicity through the shape of a network’s predictions along interpolation paths determined by the data. It approximates that behavior with orthogonal polynomials, producing a compact representation of the predictive function.

The key quantity is the representation’s effective degree: a measure of the polynomial complexity needed to describe the network’s behavior along those paths. Because the paths depend on the data, the measure accounts for the distribution being studied. The authors find that effective degree predicts generalization across tasks and architectures and consistently outperforms existing proxies such as sharpness.

The same representation also produces a differentiable simplicity regularizer, allowing the measurement to influence training directly. The authors report consistent generalization improvements in image and text classification, contrastive vision–language model fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning. The contribution therefore links a practical way to quantify predictive simplicity with an optimization signal that improves performance in the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-quantifying-and-optimizing-sim.tldr: Data-dependent polynomial representations provide a simplicity measure that predicts generalization and a regularizer that improves it in reported experiments.

paragraphs: A language model may need to follow different behavioral and safety rules in different applications, and those rules can change over time. This paper frames that challenge as specification alignment: following the particular requirements of the current scenario. It studies whether additional deliberation at inference time helps models reason about those requirements.

The authors introduce SpecBench, covering five scenarios, 103 specifications, and 1,500 prompts. They evaluate 15 reasoning models and 18 instruction models with several deliberation methods, including Self-Refine, TPO, and MoreThink. The benchmark exposes alignment gaps, while the experiments show that test-time deliberation improves adherence to the supplied specifications.

Building on those methods, the paper proposes Align3, which uses hierarchical reflection and revision to reason about specification boundaries. It advances the measured safety–helpfulness trade-off frontier with minimal overhead. The findings support deliberation as a practical way to improve scenario-specific compliance, with the benchmark providing a shared framework for examining both behavioral requirements and safety constraints rather than assessing them in isolation.
icml-2026-reasoning-over-boundaries-enha.tldr: SpecBench measures adherence to scenario-specific rules, and Align3 improves the safety–helpfulness trade-off through inference-time reflection and revision.

paragraphs: Vision–language models can produce statements that are unsupported by an image. This paper studies activation steering as a way to reduce those hallucinations during generation. Its central observation is that visual information affects token predictions sparsely and locally, so averaging image-related signals across an entire answer can weaken the most useful steering directions.

Token-Level Visual-Sensitivity Steering, or TLVS, extracts and refines steering vectors at the token level. It then adapts intervention strength at each decoding step according to visual sensitivity. This targets hallucination-prone spans while preserving content grounded in visual evidence. The method requires minimal calibration training and is designed as a lightweight component usable across different vision–language models.

The authors evaluate TLVS on POPE, AMBER, CHAIR using COCO, MMHal, and HallusionBench, reporting consistent improvements over previous steering methods. These findings support matching the timing and strength of an intervention to where visual evidence actually influences generation. They also address the paper’s concern that fixed-strength steering can unnecessarily perturb tokens that do not need correction.
icml-2026-steer-where-it-matters-token-l.tldr: TLVS reduces visual hallucinations by adapting activation steering to the tokens and decoding steps most sensitive to image evidence.

paragraphs: Connected autonomous vehicles can extend their sensing range by combining information from other vehicles. That collaboration also creates an opening for malicious participants to submit adversarial information. The paper argues that defenses based on agreement among final outputs can miss stealthy attacks and can mistake environmental noise for malicious behavior.

Cerberus instead checks consistency within the internal feature maps used for perception. It measures conflicts along three dimensions: topological structure, semantic direction, and energy distribution. These checks provide several views of whether shared features fit together, giving the defense information beyond whether the final predictions look like statistical outliers. The framework uses those signals to detect perturbations and provide dynamic protection.

The experiments report substantial improvements over state-of-the-art defenses, with attack success rates as low as 0.05% and restored average precision of 0.88. These are reported experimental outcomes rather than a guarantee for every attack. They support the paper’s central proposal that internal feature consistency can be a useful basis for protecting collaborative perception.
icml-2026-the-latent-guardian-defending-.tldr: Cerberus detects attacks on collaborative vehicle perception by checking structural, semantic, and energy consistency within shared feature maps.

paragraphs: Video inpainting must fill missing regions while keeping both individual frames and motion across frames coherent. Diffusion methods can reconstruct strong frame-level detail yet produce temporal inconsistencies. This paper examines those inconsistencies through the stability of time-indexed latent denoising trajectories, treating the generation process itself as the place to intervene.

The proposed framework monitors deviations after accounting for motion and applies corrections only when instability accumulates. Sparsely sampled trajectory anchors provide reference points, while propagation across consistent neighborhoods regulates how trajectories evolve. Implemented as a lightweight layer inside the sampling loop, the method selectively pulls unstable trajectories toward motion-consistent behavior while preserving local freedom to generate detail.

The experiments report consistent improvements in both temporal coherence and structural fidelity. This matters because stronger temporal constraints can otherwise compete with detailed reconstruction. The results support monitoring and correcting instability selectively during inference as a way to improve that balance, using the evolving denoising trajectories to determine where stabilization is needed.
icml-2026-trajectory-stabilized-inferenc.tldr: Selective stabilization of denoising trajectories improves reported temporal coherence and structural detail in diffusion-based video inpainting.

paragraphs: Graph-learning systems can lose robustness or fairness when their connections, node features, or labels change. DICT treats such perturbations as uncertainty about the data distribution. It seeks a model that minimizes the worst-case risk over a specified set of possible distributions, bringing several sources of graph uncertainty into one optimization objective.

Directly solving that objective would require an infinite-dimensional optimization problem. The authors use strong duality and local Lipschitz continuity of the loss to reformulate it as a finite-dimensional min–max problem. This step makes the framework tractable while retaining its focus on adverse shifts represented by the uncertainty set.

The paper develops robustness and fairness as its main applications, expressing fairness requirements through an uncertainty set so both objectives fit the same framework. Experiments across diverse benchmarks and model backbones show consistent improvements in robustness and fairness. The results support uncertainty modeling as a shared approach to these two properties, with the formulation also intended to provide modeling principles for broader trustworthiness objectives.
icml-2026-uncertainty-constrained-trustw.tldr: DICT unifies graph robustness and fairness through tractable worst-case optimization over distributional uncertainty.

paragraphs: Vision–language–action models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot behavior, but aggregate performance can obscure where their capabilities fail. VLA-Arena separates evaluation difficulty along three axes: task structure, language commands, and visual observations. This lets researchers probe different sources of difficulty systematically rather than treating every failure as the same problem.

The benchmark contains 170 tasks across 11 suites covering safety, distractors, extrapolation, and long-horizon behavior. Each suite has three task difficulty levels, with fine-tuning restricted to the easiest level. Language and visual perturbations can be applied independently as diagnostic probes, helping distinguish robust grounding from dependence on familiar patterns.

Evaluations reveal memorization-related generalization failures, superficial visual perception, and neglected safety constraints. Model rankings also reverse across difficulty levels, showing that easier and harder tasks provide different information. The released framework includes task definition, automated evaluation, and fine-tuning datasets. Together, these components support reproducible investigation of capability boundaries and show why success on the easiest setting alone gives an incomplete picture.
icml-2026-vla-arena-an-open-source-frame.tldr: VLA-Arena varies task, language, and visual difficulty to expose generalization, perception, and safety weaknesses in robot models.

paragraphs: Test-time defenses for CLIP aim to preserve performance on clean inputs while resisting adversarial ones. This paper finds that the reported robustness of six recent methods is substantially overestimated under basic adaptive attacks. It identifies a shared dependency: a measurement intended to distinguish clean from adversarial inputs determines whether a defense changes the original model’s prediction.

The authors argue that this assumed distinction is a fundamental weakness and introduce CLIP-MAD to exploit it. The attack targets the premise behind the defense’s decision signal, efficiently expanding the adversarial distribution without costly full gradient calculations. It can also be combined with existing attack baselines to increase attack strength.

Across 13 datasets, CLIP-MAD produces adversarial examples that markedly reduce the robustness of diverse test-time defenses. The findings show that a defense’s apparent success can depend on whether its clean-versus-adversarial indicator remains informative against attacks designed around it. They therefore challenge the evaluated robustness claims by testing the assumption that controls when protection is activated.
icml-2026-you-dont-protect-if-you-dont-e.tldr: CLIP-MAD undermines test-time defenses by attacking the assumed distinction used to decide whether an input needs protection.
